string-array.name: municipalities_array
string-array.item: Beijing is the capital of China and one of its four municipalities governed directly by the central government. Located in northern China, it combines a long history with the institutions of a modern national capital. The city is an important centre for politics, culture, international exchanges, science and technology. Visitors can explore the Palace Museum in the Forbidden City, the imperial gardens of the Summer Palace and the ceremonial buildings of the Temple of Heaven. The Badaling section of the Great Wall lies to the northwest. These sites offer different ways to discover the architecture, landscape and history of Beijing.

Shanghai is a municipality on the eastern coast of China, where the Yangtze River reaches the sea. It is part of the Yangtze River Delta and has developed into a major centre for finance, trade and shipping. The Huangpu River separates Pudong from Puxi, linking several of the best known views of the city. Along the Bund, historic buildings face the modern towers of Lujiazui across the water. Visitors can also explore Yu Garden, walk along Nanjing Road or discover neighbourhoods with older architecture. The white magnolia is the municipal flower, reflecting another distinctive part of the identity of Shanghai.

Chongqing is a municipality in southwestern China, on the upper reaches of the Yangtze River. Its central urban area developed around the meeting of the Yangtze and Jialing rivers. Mountains, hills and waterways shape its distinctive landscape, giving it the familiar name of Mountain City. The municipality extends far beyond the central skyline and includes towns, agricultural areas and mountainous countryside. Numerous tributaries flow through its valleys, while the wider region contains gorges, caves and other karst landforms. Chongqing is also an important centre for industry, commerce and transport, connecting its varied urban and rural areas through a broad regional network.

Tianjin is a coastal municipality in northern China, close to Beijing and the Bohai Sea. The Haihe River runs through the city and has played an important role in its development. Connections between the river, the Grand Canal and the sea helped Tianjin grow as a gateway for the capital. Today, Tianjin Port in Binhai New Area supports a wide range of international shipping routes. High speed rail connects the city with Beijing, while its airport and rail stations provide further transport links. Visitors can see the Tianjin Eye, explore riverside scenery and discover streets with historic buildings from different architectural traditions.
